title: Settlement Economy: production, consumption and trade of goods
about: The design: the statement (statement.md) as elements, each quoting its text, and the decisions that refine it. plan.json implements it: every feature names the design elements it serves, and tools/check_plan.py reports any element no feature serves.
source: statement.md (verbatim from the user, prompt M16 in requests.json)
summary: Resources stop being map tokens that a civilization either has or lacks. They become **goods measured in physical quantities**: tonnes of wheat, dairy and coal, bales of cotton, crates of arms. Each settlement **produces** goods from the land it works, its improvements, its buildings, its specialists and its population. It **consumes** them in proportion to its size and way of life. Surpluses and shortages drive growth, contentment, industry, trade and war. Diplomacy moves from leasing a resource for gold per turn to **real commerce**: shipping goods, selling seeds and breeding stock, and negotiating multi-part contracts.

elements.text: 1. **Physical quantities.** Every good is counted in units that mean something (tonnes, bales, barrels, crates) and is conserved: it is made, moved, stored, used up or spoiled. Nothing appears from nowhere.

2. **Production comes from the whole settlement.** Output combines worked tiles and their improvements, buildings, specialists and available labour. Land sets what is possible; people and capital set how much of it is realised.
3. **Consumption comes from population.** A settlement of a given size needs a plausible amount of food, fuel, clothing and comforts. Needs rise with size and with era.
4. **Industry transforms goods.** Factories turn inputs into outputs at defined rates, and the scarcest input limits the result.
5. **Military power has a material cost.** Units are built from production and goods, and armies in the field use supplies.
6. **Trade carries the goods themselves.** Civilizations exchange goods, the means to produce them (seeds, livestock, techniques), money and treaties, in deals of any shape.
7. **The simulation lives in the DLL.** The game's rules run in the DLL; XML holds the data and Python shows it to the player.
**Today's resource types become entries in this catalogue.** No good sits on a map plot.
**Tiles:** the land's qualities for that good (climate, soil, ore grade, fishing grounds), times the improvement built on the tile.
**Labour:** citizens working tiles produce raw goods. Specialists produce specific goods or multiply buildings' output, for example a miller, a smith or an engineer.
processing (a mill makes flour; a dairy turns milk into cheese and butter);
storage (granary, warehouse);
industry (foundry, textile mill, arsenal).
**Technology and policy:** multipliers on yields, and new production methods.

**Effects of being supplied:** a need that is met adds to growth, health and contentment, with diminishing returns. A shortfall causes hunger, illness, unrest and lost production. Larger settlements need proportionally more, so a single shipment of coffee no longer satisfies an empire.
**Stocks** sit in the settlement and are limited by its storage buildings. Perishable goods (fish, dairy, fruit) decay unless preserved.
**Within a trade network,** surpluses flow to shortages automatically, limited by roads, rivers, ports and harbours. A blockade or a cut road changes what reaches a city.
**Recipes:** buildings convert inputs into outputs at set rates and capacities. For example, 2 iron ore and 1 coal make 2 steel; 1 steel and 1 sulphur make 1 crate of arms.
**Units** cost production plus goods, such as muskets, horses, steel and fuel. In later eras, armies in the field draw supplies, so industrial capacity and supply lines become part of warfare.
| Goods | 50 tonnes of wheat; 10 crates of arms; coffee | Physical: shipped and used up |
| Means of production | Coffee seeds, breeding cattle, silkworms, mining or brewing techniques | Knowledge or stock: the buyer can then produce it |
| Money | Lump sum, instalments | Financial |
| Agreements | Open borders, alliances, rights to fishing grounds, exclusivity clauses | Political |
**Spot deals:** one shipment, delivered now.
**Supply contracts:** a quantity per turn for a set term at an agreed price, with penalties for failing to deliver.
**Packages:** any combination. For example: 20 tonnes of grain per turn for 30 turns, plus coffee seeds, in exchange for iron ore, open borders and a lump sum.
**Delivery is physical.** Goods travel by land or sea routes. Distance, ports and blockades affect what arrives, and war can break contracts.
The AI values a good by its **marginal value**: what one more unit changes in its own settlements' growth, contentment and output.
Gold is valued at what it can buy.
It also weighs the strategic cost of giving a rival the means to produce a good, for example selling seeds versus selling the harvest.
Prices come from supply and demand among trading partners. That rewards monopolies, specialisation and stockpiling, and lets the player see why a good is valuable.
**XML:** the goods catalogue, needs per citizen, building recipes and capacities, specialist outputs, and unit costs.
**Python:** the settlement goods screen, trade and contract views, and map overlays of land qualities.

**The bridge to the existing engine:** a settlement that is supplied with a good also holds the matching resource count. That keeps existing building requirements, the AI and the trade screen working while the new systems are built. I checked in the code that a city's resource count reaches its trade network.

decisions.question: Scale of units
decisions.choice: Real quantities in whole integers, each good in its own unit (tonnes, bales, barrels, crates), sized so no value can overflow; never shown as a fulfilment ratio.

decisions.question: Food
decisions.choice: Staple food is a good in tonnes. A city eats first and grows from its surplus; citizens starve only when stores are empty. Spoilage of food depends on the preservation technologies the owner lacks.

decisions.question: Number of goods
decisions.choice: The game's existing resource types, plus three new goods: Timber (from lumber camps and lumbermills on forest), Dairy (from cow and sheep pastures) and Leather (from horse, cow and sheep pastures). Extended by D28 (M59): Meat, Bread, Cheese, Cured Meat, Cured Fish, Dried Fruit, Cloth, Charcoal, Tools, Arms, Jewellery, Machinery.

decisions.question: Need tiers
decisions.choice: Needs grow along two building chains the game already has. The essentials buildings (Settlement, Town, City, Metropolitan) set how much a citizen needs of the basics (staple food, fuel, clothing). The market chain (Market, Fair, Commodity Market, Commercial Center, Hypermarket) sets which further goods a citizen wants and how much (variety, comforts, luxuries). Technological progression raises output through the techs' existing yield changes.

decisions.question: Spoilage and storage
decisions.choice: From the start, with D2.

decisions.question: Distribution
decisions.choice: As the game works now: goods are shared across a connected trade network (CvPlotGroup: roads, rivers, coast). Blockades count: enemy ships blockading water plots take them out of the network (CvUnit::updatePlunder, CvPlot::isTradeNetwork), which changes what reaches a city and what deliveries arrive. Transport limits apply only to units (their cargo), not to goods.

decisions.question: Contracts and the trade screen
decisions.choice: Modify the executable's diplomacy screen through the DLL (item list and item text); no separate trade screen.

decisions.question: Order of work
decisions.choice: Geography and the way tiles work first (component LQ), then the goods accounts and production.

decisions.question: Icons
decisions.choice: Every good keeps its icon; no icon is missing or shared. New goods get their own button, art define and glyph in both font atlases (GameFont.tga, GameFont_75.tga), made with the repository's art studio (tools/civ4-art-studio) from realistic photographic textures whose licence allows use in the mod; the source and licence of each image are recorded.

decisions.question: Wool
decisions.why: Nothing places, gives or uses BONUS_WOOL today (catalogue.json), yet clothing needs it
decisions.choice: Sheep pastures yield wool, beside meat, dairy and leather.

decisions.question: Resources that are not physical goods
options: outside the goods accounts: Drama, Music, Movies stay building-given resources; Ancient Temple and Thermal Vent stay map sites
decisions.why: They are culture given by buildings or sites with no improvement that trades them (catalogue.json)
decisions.choice: Ancient Temple and Thermal Vent stay map sites outside the goods accounts: the Thermal Vent as an electricity source, the Ancient Temple for archaeology. Drama, Music and Movies are goods (entertainment media, valuable), to be reworked; how is D21.

decisions.question: Fuel before coal
decisions.why: No timber or wood resource exists; the existing fuel goods are coal, oil, uranium, diesel, methane, biofuel and whale (catalogue.json)
decisions.choice: Timber is the fuel before coal: the fuel need applies from the start, met by timber, then coal, then oil.

decisions.question: Clothing in the early game
decisions.why: These are the only existing clothing goods (catalogue.json)
decisions.choice: The clothing goods are wool, leather, fur and cotton.
decisions.source: follows from R1 (wool and leather added)

decisions.question: How the four goods are consumed before the goods accounts exist
decisions.why: The goods accounts and needs (CN) come after production and food; until then the game consumes resources only through buildings, corporations and units. The mod already models the need tiers of D4 with those rules (GitLab main 71de0ab): each essentials building (Settlement, Town, City, Metropolitan) gives Fur +1 happiness and Cow, Deer, Pig and Sheep +3 % food each, and a city holds one of them at a time: RoMEventManager.onBuildingBuilt removes the earlier levels when the next is built (setNumRealBuilding), as it does along the market chain, where the Commodity Market gives +5 % and the Commercial Center +8 % food per livestock good and Market and Fair none; the Drapers Guild, its guildhall and Emperor's Clothes take the clothing goods, the Grocers Guild and Big the foods, the Equestrians Guild horses, the Carpenters Guild only guild paper. Effects keyed to a resource keep working through the bridge (AR.bridge) once goods are counted.
decisions.choice: Each new good is consumed by the mod's existing consumers of its nearest peer, with the peer's effect sizes. Wool and Leather (clothing, D13; peer Fur): +1 happiness from whichever essentials building the city has, +1 at the Drapers guildhall, inputs of the Drapers Guild and Emperor's Clothes; Leather also of the Equestrians Guild (harness). Dairy (food; peer livestock): +1 health of its own, +3 % food from the essentials building, +5 % with a Commodity Market or +8 % with a Commercial Center, +1 % with a Cannery, inputs of the Grocers Guild and Big. Timber has no peer: input of the Carpenters Guild, and +3 % production from the essentials building, the livestock pattern applied to production because timber is every city's fuel and building material (D12). NUM_CORPORATION_PREREQ_BONUSES rises from 6 to 8 so that full consumer lists keep every existing input. Sheep keeps its place in these consumers (D15).
decisions.correction: M29: the essentials and market buildings do not add up; one level is held at a time (RoMEventManager.py, building upgrade lines, read 2026-10-26). The effect sizes above are per city. H13 (register, append-only) and the message of GitLab e694caf0 say 'cumulative'; that is wrong. The XML is unaffected: it copies the peers' entries.

decisions.question: Livestock and crop resources once their products are goods
decisions.why: The trade design counts means of production as tradeable: coffee seeds, breeding cattle, silkworms (TR.means). The user: "Keep sheep, we need to have seeds and cattle" (M27).
decisions.choice: Sheep, and the other livestock and crop resources, stay goods: they stand for the breeding stock and the seed that trade carries as means of production. Their products (wool, dairy, leather, meat) are goods beside them, not instead of them, and Sheep keeps every consumer it has.

decisions.question: What a good is for
decisions.why: The statement gives goods a part in every system: needs per citizen that rise with size and era (3.3), processing and industry (3.2, 3.5), storage and spoilage (3.4), supplies and unit costs (3.5), trade in goods and in the means to produce them (4.1). proposals.json gave each good one need, and D14 copied the consumers of one peer, so Wool and Leather became happiness only, Dairy a few percent of food and Timber a few percent of production (M31). The first answer to that leaned on unit requirements (M33).
decisions.choice: Each good carries a list of roles in proposals.json, one per system it takes part in (role_kinds: need, material, fuel, storage, supplies, trade, means), with the existing buildings and units it touches and its substitutes. The need is one role among them. The systems' features (CN, PR.F3, SD, IN, TR.F3) take their data from these roles. Units are one consumer among buildings, households and trade. First written for Timber, Wool, Leather, Dairy, Sheep, Cow and Horse.

decisions.question: What of those roles today's engine expresses until the goods accounts exist
decisions.why: Checked in the DLL and the schemas at GitLab e694caf0: a building can have its construction sped by a good the city has (BonusProductionModifiers, CvCity::getProductionModifier(BuildingTypes), the Stone, Marble and Lead pattern), so can a unit (the Copper and Iron pattern); a building can change happiness, health and food, production or commerce percentages by good; a building or unit can require goods. There is no shortfall, no substitution among goods, no scaling with size, no spoilage, no consumption per turn and no supplies. Rules in Python are excluded by principle 7 (P7). A requirement before Timber, Wool, Leather and Dairy have producers (R7) locks content away.
decisions.choice: The bridge expresses each role through one mechanism, applied by rule to every good with that role, not hand-picked consumers: the need role as the good's own health or happiness and the essentials or market building's effects (as LQ.F12); the material role as construction speed of the buildings and units made of it (15 %, the step of Lead on buildings and of Copper and Iron on units); the fuel role in workshops as the workshop's step for each of its inputs (the Forge gives +25 % production for each of Copper, Iron and Lead). Shortfalls, substitution, size scaling, spoilage, recipes, parchment, supplies and means of production wait for CN, SD, IN and TR. No new requirements in the bridge.

decisions.question: Order of work: goods economy or land qualities first
decisions.why: Land qualities (LD.F1-F7) are the deepest and riskiest change, and in the earlier order nothing of the goods economy reached the player until they were done. The user: implement the deep change gradually, and stay grounded in the actual codebase against drift (M35).
decisions.choice: The goods economy is built first on today's resource tiles: groundwork (GW), production from placed resources and their improvements (PR), food (FG), needs (CN), storage and distribution (SD). Land qualities follow and swap the source of production from placed resources to the land. Each feature keeps its code anchors in the real source, checked by tools/check_plan.py against the mod checkout and the code map.

decisions.question: Lumber
decisions.why: Timber is essential (M31, M35): fuel and building material of every early settlement.
decisions.choice: A lumber camp on forest from Metal Casting; it upgrades to the existing lumbermill at Machinery. Bronze Working, Iron Working and Mathematics each raise lumber output (under today's engine: the tile's production, +1 per tech, the mine's step; with the goods accounts: timber per worked camp). Timber's reveal and trade techs move from Bronze Working to Metal Casting, so a camp's timber counts as soon as it is built (M36). Yields under today's engine (M39): the lumber camp has no base yield and +1 production at each of Bronze Working, Iron Working and Mathematics (3 at most); Machinery does not raise the camp, it opens the lumbermill. The lumbermill gives Timber too and its production goes from 2 to 5 (M41). Open: the user wants the lumbermill to do much better 'within the right context'; how much more, and in which context (river, later techs, timber quantities with the goods accounts), is to be settled with LD and the goods accounts.

decisions.question: Products of pastures and estates
decisions.why: A herd yields more than one good (M28, M35); latifundia are greater rural estates.
decisions.choice: A pasture, and each Latifundium stage on the same animal, yields every product of its animal: sheep: wool, dairy, leather (and the sheep itself); cow: dairy, leather; horse: leather; pig: meat only. Under today's engine a city has or lacks each good; quantities come with the goods accounts, and shortages can be filled by distribution, trade routes and imports (SD.F3, TR), which may need allocation work. Hunting camps on sheep, cows and horses give Leather, not Wool or Dairy (M41).

decisions.question: Entertainment media as goods
options: finished goods made by their buildings (Broadway, Rock'n'Roll, Hollywood) in quantities and consumed as comforts by the market chain
services: produced and consumed in the same settlement or network, not stored or shipped
keep today's form (a building gives the resource) until CN, then decide
decisions.proposal: keep today's form until CN, then decide
decisions.why: The user: still valuable goods, but maybe reworked (M35)

decisions.question: Goods catalogue fields now
decisions.why: Fields whose meaning is not fixed should not be built (rule A); spoilage, storage and value need the working goods system to be judged (M50).
decisions.choice: Each resource record gets its unit and category now, as proposed in proposals.json (M50, question 1). Storage limits, spoilage (and its representation per preservation technology) and base values wait until the goods system works (GW.F3, GW.F5); no fields for them before then.

decisions.question: How much a worked tile produces (R10, M53)
decisions.why: The user: output from the real population employed, the true efficiency given technologies and resources, land quality and the kind of good, somewhat true to a real agricultural economy
options: the model in proposals.json production: area worked (workers x hectares per worker, capped by the tile) x yield per hectare x land quality x (1 - seed), with the game's farm techs as the stages
decisions.proposal: the model in proposals.json production. Decided (M54): flows per year while turns last a year or more, the turn's fraction of a year below that; workers from the game's real population per citizen. Corrected (M54): Fermentation raises the food value of cereals and how they keep, not the harvest. Decided (M55): each map or scenario declares its area per tile (option i); the mod's scenarios and map scripts are edited automatically to declare it (PR.F6). Open: none in the model; the per-map values are data (PR.F6.T3)
decisions.choice: the model in proposals.json production. Decided (M54): flows per year while turns last a year or more, the turn's fraction of a year below that; workers from the game's real population per citizen. Corrected (M54): Fermentation raises the food value of cereals and how they keep, not the harvest. Decided (M55): each map or scenario declares its area per tile (option i); the mod's scenarios and map scripts are edited automatically to declare it (PR.F6). Open: none in the model; the per-map values are data (PR.F6.T3)

decisions.question: What a map declares in its BeginEconomy block, and how map, XML and game options layer (R12, M56)
decisions.why: The user: the block can carry many values so the game need not precompute them per tile; ideas: finite ore deposits, fertility ranges, starter seeds, trade-route settings, switchable economy screens and mechanics tied to civics
facts: The block is read by the mod's CvWBInterface.py after the base game's reader has finished (a1d9c3f2), so it can grow without breaking the base game; the harness converter (wbs2scn.py) and the WorldBuilder save must carry every key it gains
Map scripts generate their maps and have no file to hold such a block: their values come from functions (as getPlotAreaKm2) or from rules applied to what they place

The plan already has: ore grade and depth per ore good, and suitability per crop and herd good, saved with the plot (LD.F1), built from each resource's placement rules (LD.F2) and seeded from the resources a map placed (LD.F3); means of production traded as seeds and breeding stock (TR.F3); goods accounts per city with a stock per good (GW.F3)
Revolution is switched by a game option (GAMEOPTION_NO_REVOLUTION, CIV4GameOptionInfos.xml) and configured in Assets/Config/Revolution.xml, which init.xml loads
options: Layering: defaults in XML (terrain, feature and resource records: fertility ranges, deposit sizes, seed stocks) -> a map script's or scenario's map-wide values in the block -> per-plot values in the block keyed by x,y (a deposit's reserve, a field's fertility) -> the game state, saved with the plot and the city
Ore: a deposit per ore resource the map places, with a finite reserve that mining draws down (new; LD.F1 has grade and depth, not depletion)
Seeds: starting stocks of means-of-production goods per player or city, so they can be traded from turn 1 (TR.F3 with GW.F3 accounts)

Economy screens and mechanics as game options and a Config/Economy.xml, as Revolution does: import/export trade, loans and bonds, a national budget (hurry from a central panel), national debt, central planning; some opened by civics (a Roman senate), with the AI reading them
decisions.proposal: Record now, design when each part's component comes: the layering for LD (fertility, deposits) and TR.F3 (seeds); the screens as a new component after TR and AI, its mechanics designed with the user first (what a loan, a bond, a budget does), each behind a game option

decisions.question: Scale by land or by surface, and the sea (M57)
decisions.choice: Scale by land (map_scale.json as it is). Sea resources get their own mechanics: fish (and clams, crabs, shrimp, whales) a renewable stock that fishing draws and that collapses when overfished; pearls their own; offshore oil like an ore deposit but not quite (a reservoir drawn by wells, its rate falling as it empties, open). The sea plots need their own scale, the real sea a map shows over its sea plots, measured as the land scale was (map_georef.py), for the fishing grounds' size
facts: Sea goods in proposals.json (land 'sea'): Fish, Clam, Crab, Shrimp, Whale, Pearls; Oil is 'well' (on land today)
LD.F1 plans fishing capacity per plot

decisions.question: How the goods are shown (M57)
decisions.choice: As Anno does: each good has a category (what it is: staple food, fuel, ...) and a sector (where it stands in the economy): basic resources (seeds, timber, ore, leather and other raw goods), essential needs, artisanal products, industrial goods, luxury goods. The city screen shows an overview per sector and the resource overview of that city; the economic advisor an empire-wide overview. The screens use the game's own look and controls and are reached where the player already looks (the city screen's resource list, the domestic advisor) Sectors confirmed as proposed (M58; proposals.json sectors).
facts: UI.F1 already replaces the city screen's resource list with the goods panel
The mod's domestic advisor (Assets/Python/Screens/CvCustomizableDomesticAdvisor.py) shows a table of cities with configurable pages of columns; the finance advisor is BugFinanceAdvisor.py
decisions.open: none for today's goods; new goods get their sector when they are added

decisions.question: Food: nutrition and keeping (M57)
decisions.choice: Meat, dairy and fish give the most nutrition per tonne, so the most to satiety; they also give a strength bonus to living units (not siege equipment, vehicles, robots or other machines). Cereal products, dried fruit, fermented dairy, cured meat and cured fish keep longest and add most to the food store. Values per tonne and the bonus size are to be sourced (nutrition per kg, shelf life) Decided (M58): hitech, biological, clone, worker, settler and animal units get no protein bonus.
facts: Unit combat types (CIV4UnitCombatInfos.xml): living: recon, archer, mounted, melee, gun, spy; machines: siege, wheeled, tracked, helicopter, every ship and aircraft type, assault mech, robot, nanite, missile; unclear: hitech, biological, clones, worker, settler, animal
Fermentation raises cereals' food value and keeping (M54)
decisions.open: preserved forms (cured meat, dried fruit, cheese) need processing recipes (IN.F1) or a preservation share per good

decisions.question: The production chains: which goods are made where (R14, M58)
decisions.facts: research/economy/production_chains.md sections 1 and 3 (GitLab d2a8f756): converting buildings today use presence not quantity; four buildings make goods from nothing; two need inputs and make nothing; the Vincentz guilds are the artisan trades but make no goods; no granary, mill, bakery, smokehouse, tannery, weaver, sawmill or kiln building exists; Watermill, Windmill and Workshop improvements give nothing
decisions.proposal: research/economy/production_chains.md section 2: agricultural, artisanal and industrial chains on existing buildings, guilds and improvements; 15 new goods (Flour, Bread, Meat, Cheese, Cured Meat, Cured Fish, Dried Fruit, Canned Food, Cloth, Fine Cloth, Charcoal, Tools, Arms, Jewellery, Machinery); Cow, Pig, Sheep counted in head with Meat as the product; inputs for the four buildings that make goods from nothing; Glass from stone, not salt
decisions.choice: Decided (M59): the four buildings that made goods from nothing get inputs (Oil Refinery: oil; Aluminum Factory: bauxite; Cement Mill: stone and coal; Rubber Factory: rubber and sulphur); steel from iron and coal; machinery at the Factory (and the mechanised-farm stage); the Forge and the Factory make arms, the Forge tools (from ores: copper, iron, lead and the others, bauxite included) and the precious goods; the Armourer and the Jewellery building consume arms and jewellery, they do not make them; Bread Manufactory and Weapons Manufactory raise bread and arms output; the Cannery lengthens the shelf life of the city's goods (no canned-food good); charcoal from timber; no building per production step (the 32-bit executable's limits): the essentials stages (Settlement, Town, City, Metropolitan) carry the core functions; the city makes artisanal goods itself from its base goods and techs, from a communal economy on; mills (Watermill, Windmill) do not make flour; guilds are reworked: national rather than world wonders, an important role but not the source of goods, not a tier system; Cow, Pig, Sheep counted in head with Meat a good, Deer a source of meat too, Fur for clothing; decided (M60): 'communal economies and above' is Town Essentials ('Communal Organization' in the game's text) and above (City Essentials 'Civil Schema', Metropolitan Essentials 'Municipal Services'), Settlement Essentials being 'Early crafts and foodstuffs'; the Rubber Plant makes synthetic rubber from oil and chemicals
open: The guilds' role: not another modifier (M61); founding is once per game for a corporation (checked in the DLL); ideas A-D and three ways to make them national in research/economy/guilds/README.md sections 8-9 (recommended: techniques and skilled workers, national guilds with the world master guild as origin)
Flour and fine cloth as goods (not decided)

decisions.question: The guilds in the goods economy (M61, M62)
decisions.choice: Normal goods need no guild: technology, buildings and resources gate them, with no low-quality default. Guilds enable very specific luxury goods and master craftsmen and other highly qualified labour. Structure (option 3): a national guild per trade for each player, plus one world-unique master guild per trade where its technique originates; some guilds (the Glassmakers for example) stay once-per-game like corporations (the engine founds a corporation once, CvCity::canConstruct, M61). Techniques are carried by the Master units, traded in deals as means of production (TR.F3) and stolen by espionage. Guild goods carry quality grades, to be specified. No innovation brake: the evidence is contested (Epstein 1998 for guilds as carriers of skills and techniques, Ogilvie against, Epstein and Prak 2008 mixed and regional). No direct public-order bonus: guilds get a socioeconomic and political role with downstream effects, to be designed
open: Which guilds are once-per-game and which national
The luxury goods each guild enables
The quality grades and what they change
How master craftsmen are counted against the real population (D30)
sources: Epstein, S. R. (1998) Craft guilds, apprenticeship and technological change in preindustrial Europe, Journal of Economic History 58: https://bollettinoadapt.it/wp-content/uploads/epstein1998.pdf
Epstein, S. R. and Prak, M. (eds.) (2008) Guilds, Innovation, and the European Economy, 1400-1800, Cambridge: https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/C0D4374A3B5633EEF5A08520A30AF614
Ogilvie, S. (2019) The European Guilds: An Economic Analysis, Princeton (and her earlier papers on guilds, quality and innovation)

decisions.question: Whether a citizen should stand for that many people, and whether the game's exponential population should be replaced by a model closer to real settlement sizes; to be researched (historical city populations by era, urban and rural shares) before it is decided
facts: The game shows a city's population as size^2.8 x 1000 (CvCity::getRealPopulation): size 1 = 1,000, size 8 = 337,000, size 20 = 4.4 million, size 36 = 22.8 million
Per citizen that is 1,000, 42,224, 219,712, 632,914 people at sizes 1, 8, 20, 36
D23 (M54) counts the workers on a tile from these numbers, so one worked tile at size 36 stands for over 600 times the people of one at size 1
Harness games (P18, Mediterranean Standard, 1300 BC): median average city size 6.8 (232,000 people shown at size 7); largest real city in 2000 BC 40,000-65,000, Babylon about 500 BC 150,000-200,000
Growth needs 30 + 10 x size food per step (GlobalDefines) while the people added rise as about size^1.8; each citizen eats 3 food
Over 21 plots of Mediterranean Standard (4,470 km2), sizes 10-15 give 7-21 people per km2, near England in 1086 (9-15)
decisions.proposal: Research first: the sizes real cities reached in each era, how much of a city's land a citizen works, and what a Civ4 city with its 21 plots stands for (a city alone, or a city with its countryside); then compare with size^2.8 x 1000
options: keep size^2.8 x 1000 and count workers from it (D23 as decided in M54)
a new population curve fitted to real settlement sizes by era
a citizen as a fixed share of a population that grows by births, deaths and migration (a demographic model), the city size following from it
between 2 and 3: keep the food-box citizens and an __int64 people count per city beside them, growing toward a capacity set by citizens, era and food, with an urban share by era
decisions.research: research/economy/population_model.md (R17, M63): facts with sources in sections 1-4, readings R1-R6, options 1-4

compared_with_today:
| | Today | Proposed |
|---|---|---|
| Resource | A token on one tile; you have it or you don't | A quantity, produced and used up |
| Source | The one tile holding the token | Tiles, improvements, buildings, specialists, labour |
| Demand | None; one copy serves every city | Each settlement uses goods in proportion to its size |
| Luxury | +1 happiness per city, whatever its size | Contentment that grows with supply per head |
| Industry | Buildings need inputs present and use nothing | Buildings convert inputs into outputs |
| Units | Need a resource present | Cost goods; armies use supplies |
| Diplomacy | Lease a resource for gold per turn | Shipments, seeds, contracts, packages |
